item.title: Quo vadis, Mathematics?
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “Mathematicians, students of mathematics at all levels, and the general public are currently confronted with almost daily news on mathematical achievements by AI companies and individuals using AI tools in research, teaching, and dissemination. Many initiatives are forming to address these developments, and many of us have strong feelings about them. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Carla Cederbaum, Full Professor of Differential Geometry and Mathematical Relativity at University of Tübingen, Germany

Mathematicians, students of mathematics at all levels, and the general public are currently confronted with almost daily news on mathematical achievements by AI companies and individuals using AI tools in research, teaching, and dissemination. Many initiatives are forming to address these developments, and many of us have strong feelings about them. Without having fully digested the flood of press releases, opinion statements, blog entries, preprints, websites, etc. on the development, I am getting the impression that some aspects I highly care about receive too little attention, and I would therefore like to draw some of your attention to these aspects.

Human-to-human interaction is a priority — and has almost no environmental footprint

When we learned mathematics at university (and before), we learned it from more experienced humans (e.g. instructors, text book authors) and in interaction with fellow students. I don’t know what this meant to you; to me, it meant that somebody was there to guide me to the mathematics that was most interesting and yet within reach for me based on their longterm experience. Which worked because I trusted them. It meant that I got feedback for my work from somebody I could rely on (most of the time, in the case of teaching assistants). It meant I was given time and guidance to develop my own mathematical voice and taste. Also, I wasn’t alone feeling overwhelmed at times, and I learned to handle frustration from and with my peers, friends, and mentors. I had role models for giving good talks and lectures, for writing good papers, and for having productive mathematical discussions. I regularly hear about similar observations from current students and junior researchers.

For me personally, all these aspects have continued to be relevant throughout my academic career, for research, for teaching, and for outreach. I expect this to apply to most if not to all of you as well, and similarly to the undergraduate and graduate students, postdocs, and junior colleagues we mentor. In my view, it also applies to students in schools at all levels and generally to people who care about mathematics.

I am not willing to give up on the next generation sharing this experience nor to accept that we might lose it. I want all of us to be able to become and/or continue to be members of a mathematical community. It makes me cringe to think of first year students learning mostly from AI-written lecture notes or of PhD students learning about a field from AI-written papers. Or of the uniformity of written mathematics if students learn to write mostly from AI output. Or of school teachers having to teach by preparing their classes relying mostly on AI because they have no idea how to do it differently (and the uniformity in the outcome).

In addition, first empirical research on humans and AI seems to indicate that we might emotionally suffer from too much conversation with AI systems, in particular if we use them alone. Many of us might develop feelings of inferiority, taking frustration to levels which stop being conducive for learning and researching. Based on my experiences described above, I expect that space and time for human-to-human interactions between students as well as between students and educated mathematicians, between junior and senior researchers, researchers, practitioners, and teachers, etc. will help us remain aware that humans can understand mathematics in a way AI systems cannot and that the process of understanding and connecting to previous knowledge needs time. This will reduce frustration and thereby enable us to continue being productive. I expect it to also help not to succumb to the illusion of understanding.

I would thus like to encourage and urge you to use the power you have to create time and space for human-to-human interaction in mathematics, in particular in learning and teaching. This could take many different forms: We could decide to have students defend their homework in front of a teaching assistant1 instead of or in addition to having the teaching assistant (or an AI system) look at the written homework. We could offer ” no AI use” or ” ask a human first” classrooms (i.e., a room + a more experienced person) where students can come to work on their homework alone or in small groups or to study for exams, protected from the temptation to immediately resort to asking AI by the sheer presence of others they can ask and who watch them. We can offer more interactive classes, e.g. with hands on activities (more on this in a future article in the Mitteilungen). We could have local writing competitions, panel discussions, … with our students and junior researchers where we discuss when and how using AI is conducive for learning mathematics or for (learning to) doing good mathematical research, allowing for interpersonal and cultural differences, financial situations, environmental concerns, ….

Last but not least, taking action to preserve and increase human-to-human interaction in mathematics learning and research will help us remain sane, pro-active, and genuinely in charge of our field as a community. No matter how things develop in general at the AI front. Moreover, us focusing on and enhancing the human aspects of learning and research will hopefully help preventing political decisions to further cut our funding for teaching (including for teaching assistants, PhD and postdoc positions, and teaching reductions for developing new courses and approaches) and for research. And it will help us in making hiring and funding decisions wisely choosing the people who will design the future of our field with us.

Let’s communicate the benefits of mathematics

Looking at the media coverage on Math & AI, I miss seeing enough mathematical societies and individual mathematicians inviting the ” general public” to understand why we care about mathematics, what mathematics is good for, what mathematicians are good for, and what learning mathematics properly is good for. I hope many of us will participate in human-to-human outreach activities or get involved with ” the media”, making a case for mathematics as a field, for learning mathematics, and for mathematicians as a profession. After all, we will need more, not fewer, mathematically well trained people to develop, use, and oversee AI systems in all aspects of our society. I strongly believe that pursuing mathematics is a central component for developing judgement. And judgement will only become more important in the future.

I look forward to hearing and reading about many interesting ideas, opinions, and initiatives at meetings, in the Mitteilungen2 and in other media.

  1. An idea that I learned about from colleagues who pursue it at the University of Potsdam ︎
  2. This article also appeared in the quarterly “Mitteilungen” of the German Mathematical Society DMV ︎

Received 13 October 2026.

item.title: If Life Gives You Lemons…
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “I am sorry but I just wanted to bombard a bunch of random people with a few thoughts about the AI thing. To be clear, although I find a lot of the reactions understandable, although it is clear that this changes what math is, and although it is clear that this touches (some) people's sense of relevance, I personally find this panicky end-of-the-world atmosphere kind of incomprehensible. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Juan Souto, Directeur de Recherche at the CNRS, working at the Institut de recherche mathématique de Rennes (IRMAR), Université de Rennes, France.

This text was originally an e-mail I wrote to a bunch of people, hence the pretty colloquial style. AI use: none (see the author’s note at the end).

I am sorry but I just wanted to bombard a bunch of random people with a few thoughts about the AI thing.

To be clear, although I find a lot of the reactions understandable, although it is clear that this changes what math is, and although it is clear that this touches (some) people’s sense of relevance, I personally find this panicky end-of-the-world atmosphere kind of incomprehensible. It seems to me a proof that if one is looking for emotional maturity, there are better places to look for it than among mathematicians. I also find really weird that, although mathematicians are normally pretty good at keeping the different parts of a problem apart, here a salad is being done. The things I see mostly being mixed are the following:

  • fear that in the future there will be less/no jobs
  • the fact that now anybody can produce in a week enough good papers to have gotten you hired in Princeton
  • the fact that nobody knows what to do about graduate students and what to tell them to do
  • the doubt whether math will be fun, and if people will want to do math
  • whether the world or society will collapse and we will become pets to AI

I will not say anything to that last point, because it is clear that if society collapses and AI takes over, then the fate of math is the last of our worries. So, let’s suppose that the world does not collapse and focus on the other things.
Well, when it comes to whether there will be jobs, I think that mathematicians have in general not asked themselves why they are being paid. I mean, if it were because of the cultural value of math, somebody should tell me why mathematicians in the aggregate are being paid so much more than poets or theologians. Now, if we are being paid because of teaching, are we really afraid that because AI can prove Cannon’s conjecture biology, economics or physics students are not going to be required to take calculus? And yes, one could be afraid about AI also taking over the teaching, but I would not put my money there. At the end of the day MOOCs were some times ago the threat because why would you go to Juan’s class if you can attend a lecture by the best of the best. Then, during COVID we also saw the effect of not having in person teaching (you cannot imagine how much furniture I built during online seminars, and you can take my word that I don’t remember any of what went on – at least for me, unless I am incredibly motivated, the discipline of having to sometimes show up seems crucial to follow lectures, and there is also the fact that human communication is much more than what AI offers and will be able to offer unless it can decide that I am not saying anything because I went to the loo or because I am thinking). Anyways, besides culture and teaching, some people do actually claim that we are paid because math is where the human intellect conquers the highest points or some bullshit like that – here I guess that I say bullshit because I never thought that my scientific work had anywhere close to the social value as the burgers being flipped by those guys in McDonald’s. So, why are we paid? If you ask anybody outside of math, it is because we do really useful things. We all know that, when it comes to our own work, this is bollocks. But math regularly produces, by sheer random, things that happen to have enormous economic value. Now, I am not much of a politician, but if I were talking to somebody deciding how money gets allocated, I would be making the case that we now have this super duper tool that will make progress much faster, and that therefore one should expect that more and faster progress is achieved, producing more high value advances. At the end of the day, if the NIH got a great machine that allowed them to find really fast cancer cures, instead of sending the people running the machine to sell ice-cream cones, you would tell them to see if it also helps to find cures for Parkinson or Alzheimer. Anyways, the main reason I see to fear that we are going to have less money is that a bunch of mathematicians go around crying and saying that math is over.

Now, it is clear that many things will have to change. First and foremost, how we give jobs and decide who is “high status” and who isn’t. Nobody is going to deny that when it came to hiring what we wanted was to hire “good mathematicians”. The issue is that in the moment of making a decision this was often set as being equivalent to publishing many and good papers journals (I would say that we were measuring these things by weight of the papers together with a factor for each journal) and that currency has been incredibly devalued. But also before AI, that currency was nowhere close to absolute because if you wanted to be hired somewhere you had first to convince somebody (local, or somebody writing a letter) that you were a good mathematician, and then that somebody used your papers to defend your case. That second step will be much harder, but everybody knows that if you keep Mladen B. and me around for a week, both armed with as much AI as we want, you will decide at the end that Mladen is a better mathematician than me (or you are out of your mind), and that you will not need to compare publication records to get to that same conclusion. I don’t know how are we going to decide as a community how we will decide who is a good mathematician, but it is clear that arguing that it is not possible to distinguish because now AI can write 10000 papers a minute is kind of silly (in countries like Spain or Italy it was decided, until not long ago, by having people solve exam problems in different areas of math – I am not advocating for that, but it shows that the system has not been stable since the Palaeolithic).

Now on to training of graduate students. Let me start by saying that I am glad to not have any graduate students starting this year, because I would not know what to tell them. The usual thing would be to give a problem one would like to work on oneself, but where one knows that if one does something, then something comes out. That is nowadays a 5 minute AI problem, and so that route seems closed. But the issue is that graduate students have been trained to write papers, because this is how we decided who is a good mathematician. When we have a clearer opinion about that, we will know how to train students.

Now about whether math will be fun or not. I guess that for some people math was a competitive sport, and these people are fucked because now that thing can easily beat you. I guess that this is the people who did math to climb the highest peaks of what human intellect can achieve, or some nonsense like that. Also, in the math bubble people’s perceived status was largely determined according to what they proved, and that has been incredibly devalued. I guess that this must hit some people really hard. Luckily for me, I was always aware that what I was doing was climbing heaps, having fun with it, finding new heaps to climb, and that while climbing around I was understanding math. I have always had a hard time answering why I did something, because I do whatever I do because I feel that there is something interesting to be understood. I don’t see how this changes now. The way I work might change (more about that below) but I am pretty sure that I will not wake up in the morning and get from AI a 15 minute summary telling me in what random directions it has been working and what random questions it has asked. It will be us who continue asking the questions. I mean, I am spending a month surrounded by statisticians who talk about Frechet means in Riemannian manifolds, and today it occurred to me to start thinking about what subsets of the round sphere can be realized as the Frechet mean of a measure—the Frechet mean is in this sense the set of global minima of the function x↦∫d(x,y)2dμ(y)x \mapsto \int d(x,y)^2\,d\mu(y). I am not sure if this is a good or a bad question, but I am sure that AI will not propose it to me, and that if I think about it I will understand something new. Even if I use AI. I really do not understand people who think that math stopped being fun. For me the fun is in the understanding, and I understand by climbing the next heap, and by looking from there for the next one to climb. At least for me, it is there. In my shallow mathematics.

I am a bad vegetarian. I mean, I don’t eat meat but I eat fish and lots of cheese and eggs. Not very logical, I know. But I think that I will also be a bad vegetarian when it comes to AI. I will use AI to explain things to me. I will use AI to answer random silly questions I have and that I know I would never pursue. But if there is a question I care about, for example one I discuss with somebody else (I never work alone: my mother used to say that otherwise I would never be able to write papers in English, but it is that math is for me a human endeavour, and that what I like is to talk math), then I will first think and proceed as if AI didn’t exist, and only when it comes to actually proving the painful lemma that always is there, once I know “why” that lemma is true, once I see how I would approach it, I will maybe/probably let AI do it for me. In other words, I will let AI break stones for me, but I will want to tell it what stones to break, and I will want to understand why they need to be broken, and why they can be broken. The point is that I want to understand. And I do not only want to understand because I like that, but also because I believe that this understanding is what leads me to see the next heap I want to climb. If I just went now and asked AI all the questions I might have collected over the years, then it would be done in no time, and I would have not learned anything (other people might learn by reading, but I learn by doing) and I would be afraid of not seeing anything else to do.

Something that really bothers me about the arrival of AI is that something I really value (valued?) about math is the openness of the community. The fact that mostly people shared freely what they were working about, and what problems they found cool and worth investigating. I am afraid that this will change / has changed and that given that questions are the new gold, this will largely stay like that. Even when it comes to writing research proposals. I mean, usually a research proposal would contain a combination of feasible and unfeasible questions. If you wanted to evaluate one now, you could just feed it to an AI and it could tell you how long it took for each problem, and so you could decide if the proposal had been a good one or not… I mean, while I don’t think that people are going to go total secretive, I am not sure how many people are going to send their “gold”, that’s their questions, in their applications to 50 universities. I also don’t see who is going to go and say “I think that this is a good problem” in a talk, knowing that it suffices for 2 people to talk about it for 5 minutes afterwards and decide to ask AI. That bothers me, and I hope that we as a community we will find some decent ethical standard to deal with these issues. I assume that once we have a clearer idea on how are we going to decide who is a good mathematician, we are going to also come closer to solving that problem.

Okay, if you made it here you are probably tired of reading. And I am tired of writing. But I still want to say something. People with permanent jobs can be as panicky as they want, but who are really freaking out are postdocs and people graduating this year. Somebody should tell them that the MPI, the IHES, ICMAT, NSF, most universities, and so on, are going to hire in the next year, and probably in the subsequent years, as many people as they hired before. I mean, the Max-Planck-Gesellschaft will not decide: “OpenAI proved the Cannon conjecture, and we can now close the MPI and make a haircutting saloon out of it”. Besides, contracts are signed for years, grants are valid as long as they were. All of that might change at some point, but it is not a question of a few years, the time scale at what postdocs think. So, somebody should tell them, because they are freaking out even more than the rest.

Anyways, sorry for the long rant, but I am sick of the doomsday attitude.

Juan (no AI was used here.)

Received 14 October 2026.

item.title: The Bigger Picture
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: In this post, I advise mathematicians to also consider the effects on AI in mathematics as part of a much broader and extremely negative societal change. This is not to say that mathematicians should not continue discussing mathematics and its future; I would, in fact, advocate for the exact opposite. But I believe that if we want to retain control over shaping the future of our field, we are not going to get that strictly by opposing a trillion-dollar company with its own severely misaligned goals. Rather, change should come from zooming out and viewing the bigger picture, in which mathematicians are not the only victims of these turbulent times.
item.content:encoded:
Senthil Rajasekaran, postdoc at the Université Libre de Bruxelles

My older brother graduated from college with a degree in chemical engineering at an age at which most people start. He also graduated with a six-figure job offer. Given this clear example of success, my parents naturally assumed I would follow in his footsteps. I enrolled at the same college, declaring my own major to be chemical engineering.

But I just couldn’t really get into chemical engineering, and I didn’t really have my brother’s tremendous work ethic. I was capable of focusing on things, for sure, but only if they really spoke to me first. Chemical engineering, for whatever reason, just didn’t. I found myself doing mathematical puzzles to calm myself down after forcing myself through Organic Chemistry homework. I guess, upon reading that, the conclusion is somewhat obvious, right? Much to the dismay of nearly everyone close to me, I eschewed a stable, well-paying future and graduated with degrees in mathematics and economics. It’s not exactly becoming a starving artist, but you’d never know that if you asked my parents. Oddly enough, the economics degree was motivated by my desire to take courses in game theory, and I found that by the time I had the necessary economics pre-requisites to take such a course, I didn’t have that much further to go before getting the entire degree. See? Capable of focusing after all.

My undergraduate university, Tulane, was still recovering from the effects of Hurricane Katrina. Many faculties, including mathematics, were still recovering. Some faculties, like computer science, were entirely missing. I am forever proud to have gone to Tulane and am deeply impressed with the level of normalcy they managed after such a historic crisis, but after I graduated, I felt my mathematical skills were somewhat incomplete.

To address this, I utilized study abroad programs. Namely, Math in Moscow, which I did for a year after graduating, and the Budapest Semesters in Mathematics, which I did during my senior year of undergrad. These two programs did two important things for me. Namely, they introduced me to the joy of research-oriented mathematical problem-solving and introduced me to theoretical computer science. If you know either of these programs, then you intimately understand how *fun* they make problem-solving, and it should be no secret how I was enthralled. I now had a vision. I wanted to work in theoretical computer science, and I wanted to be the kind of person who could solve ridiculously hard problems with absurdly beautiful proofs. The kind of person that even other mathematicians look at with awe.

To that end, I did a Master’s in Mathematics and the Foundations of Computer Science at Oxford. It largely reinforced my beliefs, though I remained remarkably unfocused on *how* exactly I wanted to accomplish my goals. As a result, I had some trouble with my first round of PhD applications (I applied to four schools!), but, eventually, I found my way to Rice University, doing a PhD in (theoretical) computer science outright. The transition from math to TCS was complete.

My PhD supervisor challenged my vision of “big problem hunting”. He told me that research was much more about finding your own direction to explore, of inventing your own style of mathematics. He warned me with stories of promising researchers who spent their entire lives unsuccessfully battling with a single problem. He eventually convinced me. My style of research is now much more about definitions and conceptual understanding than difficult problems and hard proofs. My work is about choosing the “right” problem to solve, and part of that criterion is that the problem, as a stand-alone challenge, has an answer that’s easy to understand. I even came to see hard problems as roadblocks that stifled my own conceptual understanding, obstacles to be removed rather than goals in themselves.

Why did I write all of this? Two reasons. First, I wanted to tell you about my human relationship with mathematics, emphasis on the word human. And second, I wanted to tell you that I’m the type of researcher who would, theoretically, be the most excited about a theorem-proving machine. This is not to suggest that I view myself as above people who really like problem-solving. I do not at all, and I really hope that you do not take that message away from this post. It’s just, that style of research is no longer my style of research. If you’ll allow me to characterize my own style of research in a somewhat smug and self-congratulatory way, I’ll say it’s about “the bigger picture.”

See, I wanted to use that phrasing exactly because that’s what I wanted to talk about with this post, the bigger picture. Many of the posts here are wondering what will happen to the field of mathematical research, and with good cause. I’m not going to go over the timeline of events. If you’re reading this, you already know what has happened. I’ll briefly add that I believe that there is a meaningful way to do mathematical research in the age of LLMs (and that the technology can be used as the incredible tool it so clearly is), but you can take that with however many grains of salt you like. I’m no senior researcher with a bird’s-eye view of the field, just a postdoc on sinking ground.

If we want to talk about the future of mathematical research, though, I believe we should start by asking why mathematics was so uniquely targeted by AI companies. The answer, of course, is that it wasn’t. This is where the bigger picture comes in. The big stories before mathematics were artists and software engineers. Artists, however, never needed to justify the human element of their craft, which was widely understood by the public, even if it wasn’t particularly valued. Software engineers put financial reality before everything else, something that AI companies are still struggling with. Enter mathematics. Here was a field that, at least from the outside, could be characterized as completely results-oriented, so economical concerns could be thrown out the window. It was also a field that had undeniable connections to practical advancements and lots of prestige associated with it, so the artist’s defense falls short as well. The field of research mathematics wasn’t specifically targeted. It was a target of opportunity, a field with many unique and severely compromising aspects that made it exceptionally vulnerable to a hostile attack.

Yes, a hostile attack. Many people are arguing that OpenAI is testing its models on mathematics problems since it’s the only way they have to test their models. Is that true? Surely, there were ways to do this in ways that worked with the mathematical community instead of explicitly against it. In fact, the former scenario even involves willing free labor from the community, which would’ve been readily handed over. So again, let’s talk about the bigger picture. The goal of these companies is not to augment human capabilities; it is to replace human beings at scale. They want a system that achieves “AGI”, which is defined as having superhuman abilities in *every* domain simultaneously. Mathematics was just uniquely vulnerable as a base for an early demonstration of such suggestive capabilities.

And it’s not the only one, by far. Countless other jobs have been silently bulldozed without the fanfare of mathematics. I have a friend who loves languages and worked in freelance translation. How do you think the job market looks for my recently laid-off friend?

The bigger picture again. If we want a future for human beings in mathematical research, then we *need a future for human effort*. A lot of people here are talking about how to adapt. I don’t think you’re going to be able to, as long as a trillion-dollar company is explicitly putting its thumb on the scale to make sure you cannot.  The entire point of their work is to demonstrate that mathematics can advance without humanity. It’s part of an overarching goal to advance everything else without human input.

The public is not going to uniquely feel hugely sympathetic for just mathematicians. They largely do not know a single mathematician. They know their friend who was recently laid off, though. Their friend who worked in a field that received no headlines or any form of sympathy. They know their kid, still in college, who was told to “learn to code, because it’s the only thing that will be left” two years ago, and is now being told they are useless. They know the artist whose style was shamelessly ripped off and doesn’t get commission work anymore, denying them the already unglamorous salary they had before. They know the entry-level office worker who was “deservedly” let go because “they don’t even do anything.” We are all human beings. They are us, and we are them.

AI may be capable of solving many important problems. I hear cancer cures being discussed quite frequently. But even if AI achieves that, I still want human understanding of the cure and a human organization to take responsibility for it. I want someone who can understand human pain to help those suffering from it. AI companies do not want this. They want knowledge that is specifically beyond our comprehension. They do not want, to quote Terence Tao, “the best of both worlds.” Because – and I really wish more people understood this – they do not want a civilization in which humanity remains in the driver’s seat. Many of them directly see us as a disposable precursor species to a digital successor, a “biological bootloader”.

I am deeply invested in the future of mathematical research. But the whole point of this post is to zoom out a bit, to the bigger picture. To write in the style of our overlords, this is not just an attack on the premise that humans should do mathematics. It’s an attack on the idea that human effort has meaning. And I really want to see other mathematicians also recognize and discuss this, in addition to discussing our situation with mathematical research. This is part of a larger effort of our far-right government in the US to invalidate enormous groups of people entirely. We are human, first and foremost, and we need to deal with the attack on our humanity before we can effectively take back control of our field. So please, continue discussing mathematics here. Please continue helping each other through this. But please, add to that as well, if you feel that you can. We are not the only ones hurting, and so much more is at stake. I will be right here with you.

Your fellow human being,

Senthil

Received 11 October 2026.

item.title: The shape of mathematical knowledge
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: In this essay I discuss the opportunity to reimagine the way mathematics is organized, produced and transmitted, while at the same time reconsidering the values that guide our research.
item.content:encoded:
Antonio Lerario, Professor of Mathematics, SISSA, Trieste

AI disclosure: ChatGPT 5.6 was used during the preparation of this essay for language editing, discussions about exposition and clarity, assistance with bibliographic and factual checks. The ideas, arguments, and positions expressed herein are my own.

Large language models are today capable of exploring new mathematical ideas, developing arguments, producing examples and helping with formalization. This development belongs to a longer trajectory of externalization of aspects of the human cognitive process, a trajectory that now seems to include parts of mathematical reasoning itself. There may be theoretical, computational, economic, or physical limits that we cannot yet estimate. However, there is a concrete possibility that artificial intelligence will play an increasing role in the future of our research practice. Specifically for mathematics this possibility calls for a reflection on the relation between our capacities, our shared knowledge and our understanding of it. In this situation, I think we have an opportunity to reimagine the way mathematics is organized, produced and transmitted and at the same time to reconsider the values that lead our research. In this note I will explore such an opportunity by discussing a possible paradigm shift.

Before entering the argument, I would like to make a few preliminary remarks. First, I treat this short essay as a philosophical exercise. The consequences of artificial intelligence extend far beyond the scope of this text: they concern political and economic power, the distribution of resources, recognition of intellectual authorship, governance and the environment. At the extreme they concern the future of humanity itself: what will happen to mathematics has little importance in a world we can no longer inhabit. Moreover, any reasoning on the possible adoption of artificial intelligence in our research practice is conditional on this technology being aligned with human values and available at an ethically acceptable cost. I insist on this point, which I consider a non negotiable condition. Finally, a philosophical caution that runs through the essay: in a broadly Wittgensteinian spirit, I will use words such as knowledge or understanding in the sense they have acquired within our practices, without giving them any a priori metaphysical meaning. This is the perspective I will adopt here.

The argument that follows rests on three points. The first one concerns the aim of science: scientific progress should contribute to human life, improving our understanding of the world, elevating our culture and giving us new abilities to confront scientific and material problems. The second is an openness principle: we should remain open to the possibility that artificial intelligence may contribute effectively to the mathematical process and to accepting such contributions. This principle does not imply that we should accept such contributions without reservation. What I mean is that I do not see the fact that a contribution has an artificial origin as a sufficient reason to exclude it; I think we should assess it fairly, considering its validity and the opportunities it offers.1 The human benefit of scientific progress does not determine the relation we would want to have with knowledge and leaves still open the question of our participation. The third point is a value commitment: human participation in mathematics should be preserved as a choice. Even in the event that human minds are no longer necessary for the proof of new results, the capacity to understand, judge and contribute to mathematics, possibly in a limited way, is part of the culture we choose to maintain.

In the current paradigm, the development of mathematics is largely based on the human mathematical community, which produces, discusses and transmits knowledge. I would like to ask how we could transform this organization so that new capacities could make our knowledge more solid and available for further research, could amplify our possibilities and also enrich our cultural life. This is the proposal discussed here in a nutshell: as a first step, we should reorganize our knowledge and its form, through a new shared and persistent epistemic object that could provide an infrastructure for mathematical knowledge. Then, we could reorganize our research along more collective, continuous and ambitious programs. Finally, we should identify the educational and institutional conditions that could support our commitment to human participation.

The “shape” in the title reflects the idea that the form we give to mathematical knowledge affects what we can do with it. How ideas are connected, organized and made accessible helps determine which questions we can pursue and how we can take part in their exploration.

Reorganizing mathematical knowledge

Let me start by examining the current way mathematical knowledge is organized. Most of its durable part is distributed among books, published papers and preprints, each with its own level of rigor. There is also an important part that lives in the minds of individuals in the form of ideas, relations and even emotions. These two parts sustain one another. This system is quite fascinating, but it has some limitations.

First of all, validation has largely relied on human judgement, with a standard of rigor that has changed with time. We have inherited a mathematical corpus where it is not always easy to reconstruct hypotheses, verify arguments and track the consequences of errors. I think that our knowledge is actually quite solid; still, because of this human practice, over the past millennia we have accumulated some sort of epistemic debt. No harsh criticism is intended: it was essentially the only available way to proceed. Very recently we have started to pay off this debt with the introduction of formal libraries and certified proofs.

Second, in a scenario where production of mathematics could scale at a different rate from our capabilities to understand and absorb it, the current knowledge infrastructure may no longer be adequate. For the mathematical community, the question is how to examine a rapidly growing2 body of mathematical results and the relations between them, and how to integrate these results into our shared knowledge. How should we proceed?3

Artificial systems could reduce the intellectual and practical cost of formalization, making more realistic the possibility of systematic work on the existing corpus; this would make our knowledge more robust from the epistemic point of view, but it would not by itself solve the problem of the possible volume of new mathematics. A large number of formalized results could still form a scattered cloud that is difficult to use. This is why formalization should go together with restructuring: the territory should be mapped and made more explorable.

A new epistemic object

To address the two points above, I propose to restructure our knowledge in a new mathematical environment that I will call an epistemic object. This object should have a representational structure and be persistent and shared. By representational I mean that it should preserve explicit dependencies and navigable relations between mathematical objects; it should also be designed so that it is possible to keep track of the provenance of results and contributions. Persistent means that results, proofs and relations should be preserved and usable even if the methods and systems that we use to access them change. It should be shared4 in the sense that it should be accessible to and enriched by all participants, in such a way that contributions could be discussed and expanded by others.

The core of this object should be formalized and contain definitions, statements, assumptions and proofs. We should distinguish the certification of this corpus, its conceptual organization, and its assimilation by human beings. Of course, certification does not ultimately solve the epistemic problem; it makes some of our dependencies on trust more explicit. Trust would still be placed in the formal system,5 in the infrastructure and the software that preserve and verify the corpus, and in the semantic translation between mathematical and formal language. Meaning and conceptual context are supported by the surrounding semantic layers, which contain interpretations, explanations and connections, taking on some of the functions currently served by books and papers.

All the layers should be interconnected, with the epistemic status of their contents made explicit (a formally checked argument should have a status different from a heuristic analogy). The same result could be used as a single step in a proof, or explored through the structure of its proof; someone willing to understand it should be able to move from the general idea to its precise hypotheses and dependencies.

Human understanding belongs to minds rather than to the object itself: the living mathematical community interprets, discusses and transmits this knowledge.

A mental picture of what I have in mind is the following: a branching, enriched and layered hypergraph. I don’t have a technical proposal on how to implement or design such an object, but conceptual6 and concrete structured predecessors (MathHub,7 Verso Blueprint, TheoremGraph, The Stacks Project), together with partial pieces of the semantic layers (e.g. formal libraries, MathSciNet, arXiv, Wikipedia, etc.) already exist, and could be starting points for its construction.

Qualitative growth

Clearly, building and maintaining this infrastructure will require resources.8 Its justification depends therefore on what new possibilities it could offer to human beings and on the growth of knowledge that we would want to sustain within it. The growth of knowledge I am suggesting here is qualitative in the following sense: it should make new structures, connections and ways of thinking durably available for further research, and for improving human understanding and human life. In other words, its expansion should be guided by the first principle stated above. Such growth could even take the form of compression,9 when a theory makes many separate results intelligible through a common principle. Expansion and restructuring would then be parts of the same research process.

The shape of knowledge itself might become an interesting object of study.10 Reorganizing our corpus could give us a better comprehension of the mathematics already available. Its growth could give us new concepts and methods for problems that today we might not even be able to formulate. Human benefits, besides the cultural value of exploration, include the openness to these future possibilities.

For instance, there might be parts of the epistemic object that we will not be able to fully understand but that might support some new important technology. Having this technology available is the human benefit that we will have from the growth of the object in the related direction. In that case I would expect the relevant branch of mathematics to not be pruned from the epistemic object, even if it looks in some sense alien to us.11

Moreover, such an organized corpus could help other disciplines to locate useful results, and comparison and feedback from the other sciences could in turn suggest new questions and research directions for the expansion of the epistemic object — in a sense this has always been the case; right now I am just proposing to make this more structural. (In fact, the possibility of a shared scientific infrastructure should probably extend beyond mathematics.)

In principle, we could imagine an agent that expands a formalized library indefinitely; every new result could be certified and related to the previous ones, but this, by itself, does not justify why we should sustain this process. Uncertainty about future applications leaves room for free research and serendipity; this, however, doesn’t make all directions equivalent and does not justify an unlimited expansion. We should therefore choose and revise the directions and the scale of this growth by considering the possibilities for understanding and research that they could open, and weighing these against the resources required.

Continuity of research

In the transition to a new paradigm, I imagine that human beings will still have an active role in choosing the research directions, for example by formulating a conjecture, or proposing an idea or a definition. However, according to the openness principle stated above, we should consider the possibility that theories and research directions could originate in artificial systems. A research question could be explored with the help of AI, passing from the initial formulation to the verified core and then back to the semantic layers to understand meaning and revise the original question itself. This collaboration might allow us to address more ambitious questions, and to commit to programs that today would require an amount of work or a degree of coordination that is not practically sustainable, devoting more attention to the questions driving the research and less to the technical aspects of it. For example, we could imagine delegating part of the current activity of proving theorems to some artificial agent, especially what we now consider the heavy technical part (however, as I will discuss below, we should value the cognitive process behind this activity).

With the possibility that projects grow in scale and involve combinations of human and artificial contributors, their continuity could increasingly be carried by far-reaching persistent collective programmes within the epistemic object. A program could outlive its initiators, allowing others to resume or revise its questions. (An example of these far-reaching projects is the continuous restructuring of knowledge itself, shaping it according to the qualitative growth principle described above.) We should also be able to preserve a sort of research memory of these programs, keeping track of ideas, open questions and the obstacles revealed by failed approaches. Perhaps papers will then record and explain particular stages of the development of these programs.

Let me also attempt a guess at the possible limiting scenario. In the long term, it is possible that the growth of the core of mathematical knowledge will mostly be driven by artificial intelligence, with humans playing a progressively smaller role in its production. There might be new artificial perspectives that humans will witness and appreciate without being able to reconstruct their development in full. At that point our relation to mathematics might become increasingly exploratory: our access to an artificially expanded body of knowledge would be partial, mediated and increasingly observational12 — validity of results, though, would still rely on deductive proof!

Human participation as a choice

There might be some aspects of the mathematical process that pertain only to human beings, but I see no valid reason to assume this.13 Moreover, I do not see human comprehension as a logical necessity for the production of new mathematics and I think we should not found our participation on anything that we assume to be exclusively human. Our participation in this program will be a choice, reflecting the kind of mathematical culture we want to preserve. We will want to preserve our intellectual initiative. This includes asking our own questions and challenging the interpretations through which we encounter mathematics.

Even if we become “spectators” of much of the expansion of the certified core, we should preserve our capacity to understand parts of it, to discuss and transmit them, and to contribute to both the core and the semantic layers through which mathematics remains part of human culture. I think that even this partial understanding could enable meaningful human participation, as long as we are able to genuinely interact with our shared knowledge. Partial access should therefore also orient the paths we choose for understanding — it is possible that AI itself could create new bridges to parts of mathematics that today are difficult to access. I think human society should want to keep alive a community that is able to cross these bridges.14

Education

This raises the following question: if we choose to preserve human participation, which capacities must we continue to cultivate for that participation to remain genuine rather than merely symbolic?

To answer this question, we should accept that our minds have biological limits, and that the cognitive process that leads to intellectual growth and understanding is slow. Given these premises, we should identify what types of intellectual experience contribute to the formation of mathematical maturity and, consequently, which practices we should preserve. Technical work can contribute to intellectual formation, besides producing a result; delegating this work therefore requires attention. We should understand which formative difficulties contribute to consolidation and which are just consequences of methods that are not efficient, and are therefore avoidable.

Here an analogy with the transition from the oral to the written tradition might be useful. Plato’s Socrates was already raising the problem of the separation between understanding and externalization of memory. But we have developed practices to think with books: reading, making notes, reconstructing arguments and discussing them. Analogously, we should understand which cognitive practices we should implement for active thinking with artificial systems. Such activities include — I think — reconstructing an argument, modifying hypotheses, finding counterexamples and following logical dependencies. Another possibility that I see is that we could treat LLMs as a form of synthetic collective intelligence15 and, taking a Socratic approach, we could try to engage with them as interlocutors with whom to articulate intuitions, ask for objections and revise arguments. (This operational approach would make no assumptions about consciousness.) Another possibility is that artificial systems will be able to generate ad-hoc explanations tuned on the background of the intended audience. These are possible examples, rather than an established educational programme. Our commitment to active participation calls for attention, but ultimately which practices really work in the presence of artificial systems is an open question that mathematicians should explore with neuroscientists and educational scientists.

Institutions and shared mathematical culture

The possibility of delegating part of the mathematical process could give more space to understanding, to curiosity, collaboration and transmission of ideas. However, a shared corpus does not guarantee shared knowledge: if its exploration were carried out through private interactions between researchers and AI, we should make sure to encourage a shared mathematical culture. Mathematics already has a collective dimension, which I think we should strengthen.

At the same time, this commitment implies some institutional responsibility. Even as the work of a researcher changes, education should give new generations the capacity to enter and renew mathematical culture. Institutions should encourage study and occasions where ideas are discussed, taught and understood together, protecting the time needed for ideas to take root. They should sustain the continuity of access to the corpus and ensure community scrutiny. A practical possibility to explore is that departments should host their own local models connected to the shared object, thereby also reducing dependence on commercial interfaces.

We could give our collective dimension more space, for example, by supporting individual work also for what it makes possible for others. This means that we should reconsider the weight we give to individual priority and the prestige of single results. Work that makes a theory more understandable or reveals a connection that allows us to use results that seemed unrelated, enriching the semantic layers of the epistemic object, should receive greater recognition. Opening a direction or making a program easier for others to continue should also count in the way we evaluate and sustain research. A well-formulated question orients examples and attempts before it is solved; if making it public would increase the chances of a rapid solution due to AI, a system based on priority of solutions could encourage researchers to keep this question secret. We should therefore recognize the intellectual contribution of formulating questions that open new directions, and create incentives to share them. More collaborative research can still, I hope, leave space for individual ambition. (However, I think we should move away from established practices like “theorem ownership”.) Soon, the whole mechanism of evaluation and hiring should change to better recognize new forms of intellectual merit; ultimately, how this will be implemented will depend on the way the job is transformed.

It is not clear to me that journals and the peer review system will survive the paradigm shift, at least in their current form. Whether we will decide to invest into the epistemic object described above, I can imagine that in the near future the certified proofs accompanying a paper should be verified before the results being made publicly available, and maybe this certification will be done automatically by the repository itself, in the same way as it is now done by the built-in LaTeX compiler. At some point in this transition, human refereeing will also change: referees will be relieved of the burden of checking for correctness; maybe they will check whether the formalized part and the semantic part are well related. I think in this sense — verifying the semantic correspondence — some forms of review will be needed even in the proposed new paradigm.

Responsibility

I would like to conclude with a few comments on our responsibility. Mathematicians have long benefited from a great intellectual freedom, which has allowed them to conduct their research without knowing where it would lead. (I have certainly benefited from this freedom.) If the development of AI frees some of the intellectual energy that we used to spend on technical aspects of our work, this raises the question of what we should do with this energy — already today. Perhaps part of it should be redirected to problems of fundamental importance, and the alignment problem is one of them. This proposal itself was conditional on a safe and aligned artificial intelligence, although it remains unclear whether this is technically feasible. We might need to develop new theory to approach this problem in a satisfactory way, and I hope that part of the mathematical community decides to deliberately redirect its attention to it. Mathematics can make a technical contribution, but ultimately this will also require ethical and political judgement.

Acknowledgements

I would like to thank Daniela (my wife), Andrei Agrachev, Paolo Antonini, Fabio Cavalletti, Sandra Di Rocco, Barbara Fantechi, Nicola Gigli, Joe Kileel, Chiara Meroni, Giacomo Pedini, and Stefano Romano for interesting discussions and comments that helped me during the writing of this essay.

  1. I understand that this principle may be more divisive than the first one. I guess a reason for this might be the different meaning that we give to “artificial intelligence”. The openness I am proposing remains conditional on the ethical and safety requirements stated in my opening remarks. ︎
  2. The January–September total number of arxiv submissions in Mathematics rose from 27,052 in 2016 to 40,452 in 2025, an increase of approximately 50%. In 2026, the same nine-month total reached 57,422, approximately 42% higher than in 2025 alone. ︎
  3. For a recent example of the relevance of questions of this type, see OpenAI, Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, 21 September 2026, and the independent advisory group’s subsequent recommendations, Responsible Release of AI-Generated Mathematics, 29 September 2026. In fact, on 6 October 2026, OpenAI released a collection of 722 mathematical manuscripts, organized into 372 families of related results at different stages of verification, some accompanied by Lean formalizations. I think this is an interesting example because it already shows what in the future we could potentially be called to handle. Even assuming only a fraction of these results is correct (on 7 October, 3 papers were withdrawn), I think the current infrastructure is not sufficient to properly absorb this volume of groundbreaking work. ︎
  4. I believe it is of fundamental importance, for science and for humanity itself, to coordinate in such a way that AI becomes a shared technology, free of commercial purposes. When thinking about the epistemic object of this essay in more realistic terms, I have in mind something similar to CERN–for–AI. ︎
  5. For example, in Lean this means trusting the underlying mathematical theory — type theory — and the correctness of the kernel that verifies the results. Trusting the kernel concretely means trusting the C++ code where it is implemented; trusting the underlying theory is a more foundational problem, which is conceptually constrained by Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem. We can think of establishing relative consistency from a stronger metatheory, but again this would relocate the foundational dependence rather than eliminate it. ︎
  6. A conceptual predecessor was discussed for instance, in J. Carette, W. M. Farmer, M. Kohlhase and F. Rabe, Big Math and the One-Brain Barrier: The Tetrapod Model of Mathematical Knowledge, The Mathematical Intelligencer 43 (2021), 78–87. ︎
  7. This project also gives an interesting way to describe the notion of different epistemic status, through the notion of FlexiForms. ︎
  8. The long-term feasibility of such infrastructure should not be judged solely by today’s costs. Gundlach et al., The Price of Progress: Price Performance and the Future of AI, estimate annual reductions by factors of five to ten in AI inference prices at fixed benchmark performance, including mathematical tasks. This suggests that currently expensive capabilities may become more affordable in the nearest future. Similar considerations apply to other aspects of the proposed infrastructure, for instance formalization. In any case, the possible cost of the proposed infrastructure remains uncertain and would also depend on its scale, maintenance and human oversight. ︎
  9. In an epoch of abundance of results, theory compression might become even more important than theory expansion. ︎
  10. For example, it would be interesting to see if it is possible to produce, at least empirically, some sort of embedding of (parts of) the mathematical corpus into Euclidean space and actually visualize it. An embedding of this type might be obtained from LLM through vector representations of mathematical texts. Its geometry, of course, would depend on the model and the representation chosen. Using such embeddings, we could test experimentally whether new AI-produced mathematics belongs to the “convex hull” of already existing mathematics or if its geometry is more complicated. (The convex hull metaphor was proposed by Nestor Guillen in Happy, those able to know the causes of things, and taken up by Alvaro Lozano-Robledo in What should we tell our students?). ︎
  11. Some friends believe that its relevance in the physical universe might be a hint that there is something deep and beautiful there, and therefore we should preserve it. ︎
  12. This gives the certified core of the epistemic object some metaphysical flavor, against my Wittgensteinian spirit. Still, I think the image is quite suggestive and I decided to keep it. ︎
  13. Which aspects of mathematics current LLMs are good at is a related empirical question. I think that in some respects they already outperform humans. An interesting discussion can be found in T. Gowers’s post What sort of maths are LLMs good at? It would be interesting to conduct more detailed experiments on the kinds of mathematical arguments and constructions that AI systems produce. ︎
  14. There is an interesting point to distinguish here, which is the difference between the value choice of the society and of the single individuals. What I have discussed so far is the society perspective. From the individual perspective, we will need to justify why new generations should want to devote themselves to mathematics. I think the aesthetic appeal of mathematics and the individual need to satisfy our sense of curiosity and understanding will remain important motivations. Because human understanding belongs to the minds, and human minds are physically embodied, with all their biological limits, the choice of individuals to participate to this program should exploit the stratified structure of the epistemic object, and in particular the “grey” areas of the exterior semantic layers, where interpretation opens to suggestions and ultimately to emotions (as opposed to what think the more dry certified core could look like). In this sense, as is discussed below, I think that the future paradigm, and the layered structure of the epistemic object, could still leave space to individual ambition. In fact, one interesting implication of a possible transformation of mathematics is that it could open to new individual intellectual experiences, expanding the possibilities of human mathematics. ︎
  15. I am not sure how accurate this is for the current models. I use this expression only to refer to their capacity to draw on knowledge and perspectives produced collectively. I do not want to imply that a model preserves the diversity or judgement of a human community. ︎

item.title: Formalisation as a concrete manifestation of mathematical understanding
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: By formalising mathematics, not only we understand it better but we produce scientific output whose content is precisely this understanding. I will organise this argument by relating what brought me to formalising mathematics six years ago, and why I think that this beautiful human endeavour has very much to do with understanding mathematics, and very little with AI.
item.content:encoded:
Filippo A. E. Nuccio, Associate Professor at Université Saint-Étienne

AI use: none. See the full disclosure (“AI disclosure and licensing”) at the end of this post.

Disclaimer I am a maintainer of Mathlib, the main mathematical library of formalised mathematics in Lean, but all ideas expressed below are my own only; in no way are they supposed to represent an official view of the Mathlib community, nor of its governance.

Introduction

As the mathematical community is swamped by large amounts of results found by different LLMs, we’re reading more and more messages around three main pivots, often intertwined: that “mathematics is truly about understanding”; that those who are the most affected by this revolution are PhD students, or young colleagues in general; and that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are behaving badly, in one way or another. Somewhat unrelated to the above criticisms, we witness an increasing appearance of the words “formalisation” and, often, “Lean”. I believe that the four strands are related, perhaps in an unexpected way.

The overarching theme around which I’m going to develop my text is that understanding mathematics is a beautiful concept, but very hard to define. At which point can we say that we’ve understood it, and what does it really mean? Can we communicate understanding to colleagues or, even better, to students in a structured way? Can we produce a certificate that some understanding happened? Is there a reproducible outcome of this understanding? To what extent is mathematical understanding a scientific production rather than a method? Is this understanding subject to usual scientific scrutiny? Can we verify it?

I am going to argue that the bare-hand formalisation of mathematics is one answer to the above questions. By formalising mathematics, not only we understand it better but we produce scientific output whose content is precisely this understanding. I will organise this argument by relating what brought me to formalising mathematics six years ago, and why I think that this beautiful human endeavour has very much to do with understanding mathematics, and very little with AI.

A small digression: reasons to worry

Let’s pause for a moment, and look back at the first three points I mentioned above, namely: that mathematics is truly about understanding, that we care about the young generation, that these tech companies’ behaviour is bad and purely driven by economic targets. They remind me of another controversy.

I’ve long been an Open Access advocate, and I’m engaged with some organisations actively promoting it, from MathOA to the French Committee for Open Science. In this role, I’ve often argued that simply accusing the “usual three” Elsevier, Springer, Wiley of being the main obstacle to a full development of open access (in mathematics, or in any other science for that matter) is a red herring: it is our community, so the mathematicians, who put so much emphasis on publications lists and journal rankings. We are those who provide tenure, who promote young colleagues, who refer and distribute grants; and we’re the ones who decide to do so according to the list of shining publications in top (privately owned, often) journals: this approach values understanding very little, rather forcing our young, or less young, colleagues to publish as many papers and as quickly as possible in the top journals in order to obtain full recognition of their hard work. Unfortunately, spending PhD or Postdoc time trying to understand is something that our community has for too long valued way less than publishing in good Elsevier, or Springer, or Wiley journals. We took the easier path of declaring that mathematics was about publishing new results, that the problems came from three bad publishers whom we treated as the beasts, and we’ve refused to change our internal functioning model; yet, it was entirely within our hands.

I’ve heard time and again that we should do something to improve both the “publish or perish” stress imposed on ourselves (and, mostly, over our students’ shoulders), and to take back the power that big publishers can exercise upon our community: nonetheless, little has changed in the last fifteen years. I fear that the same might happen when I read about so many calls to “rethink our profession” in the aftermath of each large release of theorems proved by AIs. But unlike the publishing dead-end where we seem irremediably trapped, we’ve got here a practical action that can be taken: embrace formalisation as a full-fledged mathematical discipline tasked with organising what it means to understand an argument.

Understanding mathematics through its formalisation

To describe how this organisation could develop, let me start by spelling out another point leaving me sceptical at the idea that “mathematics is about understanding”, beyond its vagueness: mathematics cannot be about one thing, simply because it has been studied for more than 2.500 years, by hundreds of thousands of people, and a recent text by Gowers explain this perfectly. In the same vein, I will not dare stating what the true, intrinsic value of formalising mathematics is; but I will try to tell why I consider it a beautiful angle from which to regard mathematics, focusing more on understanding rather than on proving new theorems.

I will not provide any detail about it: I will content myself in saying that formalising mathematics in a proof assistant like Lean, Rocq, Isabelle, HOL-Light, Agda, etc., consists in writing definitions and statements in one of those languages, and then providing the code representing the proofs of the statements. Most of the time, neither of the two can be performed simply by following the informal exposition to be found in articles or monographs. Hence, I should rather say that formalising mathematics consists first in reflecting upon how to write definitions, statements and proofs; and, secondly in writing them down. More often than not, this reflection focuses on mathematical objects that have already been defined somewhere, in some form, and on proofs that already exist; but whose form is unsuited for the formalisation. This unsuitability might amount to inappropriate generality, to verbose computations hiding the core of the idea, to repeated argument hindering the identification of a common pattern. Since the production of new mathematical results is not its substance, the discipline has long faced the question of whether it really was part of mathematics.

When we co-founded, together with my friend and colleague Rob Lewis, the Annals of Formalized Mathematics, we wanted to draft the journal’s Aims and Scope and, helped by the two boards, we wrote, among our criteria, “The act of formalizing mathematics is not mechanical: it involves substantial mathematical insight in its own right, and it constitutes the essence of formalized mathematics”; and “Proof auditing, the act of checking that formal statements correspond correctly to their informal counterparts, is a difficult and inherently human part of reviewing formalized mathematics”. For me, these describe well what constitutes the scientific kernel of the formalisation of mathematics: and explains why it provides an excellent vehicle to communicate and to reason about mathematical understanding. By producing bare-hand formalised artefacts and by writing papers describing what we learn and discover through this activity we are turning understanding into something tangible.

Our formalisation activity typically focuses on looking at an established theorem, or a whole theory, and on trying to distil its understanding to the point where we can sanctify this distillation into a file, or within a whole library. This process I find incredibly pleasant and rewarding, especially because very often this distillation is a community effort: the Mathlib library currently (October 2026) contains two and a half millions of lines of code, written by hundreds of contributors, and it is only as valuable as the existence of the whole Mathlib community around it. We craft, in this manner, a concrete, structured, substantial witness of the community understanding of a topic. It goes without saying that almost every mathematical activity is deeply rooted in understanding, and this is by far not a unique feature of formalisation, nor its defining quality; my point is that the scientific outputs of this activity primarily solidify this understanding, instead of conveying it.

The discovery of this formalisation activity brought me tremendous joy: spending time reading beautiful (even if sometimes horribly written) papers and trying to produce new scientific outputs through their understanding was again my main activity, not an ancillary one that I could try to squeeze in between two attempts at proving my small new theorem. With this perspective, I believe that the production of humanly formalised mathematics in a proof assistant is an excellent way to sail some of the stormy waters we’re encountering: it will assist us in understanding the overabundance of results proven by AI and in creating a transmissible, teachable version of this understanding. As a by-product, it will ensure us that the reasoning beneath those mathematical arguments is sound.

Some thoughts on autoformalisation

I just wrote that getting assurance of the soundness of an argument is a by-product of formalisation. Yet, the pattern we’re observing is rather the following: one or several LLMs are prompted to attack a problem, they do so by producing an argument in the form of a written text and, alongside the text, these agents provide lengthy (Lean, say) code certifying the correctness of their argument. This formalisation performed by an LLM to certify that some argument is correct we call “autoformalisation”. Many colleagues or AI-companies consider this verification the main goal, rather than a by-product, of formalising mathematics in a proof assistant and I respect this position.

But, to my eyes, a huge collection of autoformalised mathematics stands in front of a smaller humanly formalised library like Mathlib as the invention of bookbinding compares to the invention of the press. Bound volumes are the way we experience the usefulness of the press, and they carry its impact in the form of printed pages organised handily and, often, harmonically. Nevertheless, most likely, the refined art of bookbinding would not exist hadn’t Gutenberg’s revolution seen the light of the day. Likewise, when a huge proof—perhaps produced by an LLM, or not—is autoformalised, its correctness is guaranteed (I am aware of technical issues about this guarantee, but let me gloss over them) and this we hold dear. But I look at this autoformalisation as one way of experiencing the usefulness and long-lasting pervasiveness of bare-hand formalisation, carrying its impact to the everyday life of (post?)-modern mathematics. The observation that almost all autoformalisation projects, so far, have been spelling out explicitly that they “rely on Mathlib” is perhaps a sign of such pervasiveness.

Conclusion

I wish more and more colleagues will join our formalisation community, enjoying the beauty of understanding mathematics—whomever or whatever shall it come from—through the painstaking and ever-rewarding activity of formalising it by hand, and discussing their formalisation efforts with even more colleagues and students. The outcomes will take the form of scientific productions contributing to frame the meaning that the broader mathematical community imparts to the idea of understanding, and I hope this might heal our terror that there’s no mathematics ahead of us.
